title: Detecting and Perturbing Privacy-Sensitive Neurons to Defend Embedding Inversion Attacks

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to protect text embeddings against inversion attacks while minimizing damage to non-sensitive information, unlike prior methods that add noise to all embedding dimensions and degrade downstream utility. Papers [7], [8], and [20] address text embedding inversion attacks, but none propose a defense mechanism that specifically minimizes damage to non-sensitive information while targeting privacy-sensitive neurons. These prior works focus on identifying vulnerabilities or reconstructing text embeddings rather than defending embeddings in a utility-preserving manner. Thus, the purpose is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, DPPN (Defense through Perturbing Privacy Neurons), involves a differentiable neuron mask learning framework that identifies privacy-sensitive neurons and applies one-sided Laplace noise to those neurons. Papers [2], [3], [4], [5], [10], [16], and [19] discuss noise injection or perturbation techniques for privacy preservation in neural networks, including differential privacy mechanisms and neuron-level perturbations. For example, [4] introduces a neuron noise-injection technique for privacy preservation, and [19] discusses pruning as a form of noise injection to achieve differential privacy. While these papers use noise injection or perturbation, none propose a differentiable neuron mask learning framework or one-sided Laplace noise targeting privacy-sensitive neurons. Thus, the mechanism is **not covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves learning a binary neuron mask via differentiable relaxation and validating perturbation effects through downstream experiments. Papers [4], [5], [10], and [19] use similar evaluation designs, such as validating privacy-preserving methods through downstream utility experiments. For example, [10] applies calibrated noise to embeddings and evaluates its impact on utility, and [19] validates pruning-based privacy mechanisms through experimental results. These prior works use comparable evaluation designs, even though the specific object (DPPN) differs. Thus, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is privacy-preserving NLP/text embedding security. Papers [7], [8], [20], and [11] address privacy risks and security concerns in text embeddings, including inversion attacks and defenses. For example, [7] explores privacy risks in text embeddings, and [8] focuses on embedding inversion security for multilingual models. These papers operate in the same general application area of privacy-preserving NLP and text embedding security. Thus, the domain is **covered**.

## Purpose

The contribution's purpose is to protect text embeddings against inversion attacks while minimizing damage to non-sensitive information — specifically targeting selective protection (only sensitive dimensions) rather than uniform noise addition.

Papers [7], [8], [11] address embedding inversion attacks on text embeddings. Paper [8] explicitly discusses "defence mechanisms" for text embeddings against inversion. Paper [10] addresses "privacy- and utility-preserving textual analysis" with the explicit goal of balancing privacy and utility in text representations. Paper [30] addresses "concept erasure" — removing specific attributes from distributed representations while preserving others, which is structurally the same objective: selectively suppress sensitive information while preserving utility. However, [30] is about erasure from representations generally, not specifically about inversion attack defense. Papers [7] and [8] are closest — they address the same problem class (defending text embeddings against inversion while maintaining utility). Paper [8] explicitly mentions defense mechanisms for text embeddings.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: (1) identify top-k privacy-sensitive neurons via a differentiable binary mask learning framework, then (2) inject one-sided directional (negative) Laplace noise only on those identified neurons.

Paper [2] proposes "adaptively inject noise into features based on the contribution of each to the output" — this is adaptive/selective noise injection, but it's isotropic and not directional. Paper [19] uses pruning (zeroing neurons) as equivalent to DP noise, but doesn't use a learned mask for selective perturbation. Paper [4] injects noise into specific neurons for privacy. Paper [23] proposes per-neuron DP mechanisms. None of these combine: (a) differentiable mask learning to identify privacy-sensitive neurons + (b) one-sided directional (negative) Laplace noise specifically on those neurons. The directional (one-sided, negative) noise component is distinct from standard Laplace/Gaussian DP noise. Paper [2] is the closest with adaptive noise per neuron contribution, but lacks the differentiable mask learning and directional perturbation. No prior paper covers this specific combination.

## Evaluation

The contribution is validated by downstream NLP task experiments (utility preservation) and inversion attack resistance metrics — standard evaluation designs in privacy-preserving NLP. Papers [7], [8], [10], [11] all evaluate text embedding privacy methods using inversion attack success rates and downstream task performance metrics. This is the same evaluation design (attack success rate + downstream utility benchmark), just applied to a different method. Paper [8] explicitly uses this design for multilingual embedding defense evaluation.

## Domain

The domain is privacy-preserving NLP / text embedding security. Papers [7], [8], [10], [11] all operate in exactly this domain — privacy-preserving NLP with text embeddings. This is clearly covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to demonstrate that selective privacy-neuron perturbation yields a superior privacy-utility trade-off compared to baseline all-dimension noise methods across diverse datasets and attack models. None of the prior papers explicitly establish this specific empirical relationship. While several papers (e.g., [2], [4], [5], [9], [13]) discuss privacy-utility trade-offs in differential privacy or privacy-preserving deep learning, they do not report or demonstrate the same empirical finding that selective privacy-neuron perturbation outperforms all-dimension noise methods. For example, [4] introduces a neuron noise-injection technique but does not compare selective perturbation against all-dimension noise methods or establish the same trade-off improvement.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves empirical evaluation across six datasets and multiple perturbation levels, comparing DPPN against LapMech (Laplace) and PurMech (Purkayastha) baselines, against three attack models (MLC, GEIA, Vec2text), and on real-world sensitive datasets. Paper [4] introduces a neuron noise-injection technique for privacy-preserving deep neural networks, which is substantively equivalent to the selective privacy-neuron perturbation mechanism described here. Both approaches involve perturbing specific neurons to achieve privacy preservation, even though the exact implementation details differ. The mechanism is therefore covered by [4].

### Evaluation
The evaluation design measures relative privacy leakage reduction and downstream utility improvement across multiple datasets, embedding models, and attack models. Papers such as [9] and [13] use similar evaluation designs to quantify privacy leakage and utility trade-offs in privacy-preserving deep learning. For instance, [9] evaluates privacy-preserving mechanisms against reconstruction, tracing, and membership attacks, while [13] measures privacy leakage and utility degradation in gradient embedding perturbation. These prior papers employ comparable evaluation designs (e.g., privacy leakage metrics, utility comparisons across baselines) even if applied to different datasets, models, or attack types. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is privacy-preserving NLP evaluation. Papers such as [9], [10], [16], and [20] address privacy-preserving methods or privacy leakage in NLP or text embeddings, which is substantively equivalent to the application area here. For example, [9] investigates privacy-preserving deep learning mechanisms against privacy attacks in NLP, and [20] explores privacy risks in text embeddings. While the specific datasets or sub-problems differ, the general domain of privacy-preserving NLP is covered.

Paper [4] ("A Neuron Noise-Injection Technique for Privacy Preserving Deep Neural Networks") explicitly addresses neuron-level noise injection for privacy-utility trade-off in DNNs. Paper [5] ("Deep Learning With Data Privacy via Residual Perturbation") also targets privacy-utility trade-off improvement. However, none of these specifically demonstrate that *selective* neuron perturbation (targeting privacy-specific neurons) outperforms all-dimension noise in the text embedding/NLP context. Paper [4] is the closest — it injects noise into neurons for privacy preservation and discusses the accuracy-privacy trade-off, which is substantively equivalent to the purpose of showing selective neuron perturbation achieves better privacy-utility trade-off than baseline noise methods.

**MECHANISM: Empirical evaluation across six datasets and multiple perturbation levels, comparing DPPN against LapMech (Laplace) and PurMech (Purkayastha) baselines, against three attack models (MLC, GEIA, Vec2text), and on real-world sensitive datasets.**

The mechanism here is the empirical comparison protocol: selective privacy-neuron perturbation vs. Laplace/Purkayastha baselines, evaluated against multiple attack models. **EVALUATION: Reduces relative privacy leakage by 5%-78% while improving downstream utility by 14%-40% vs baselines; consistent across embedding models.**

The evaluation design uses privacy leakage metrics (attack accuracy) and downstream utility metrics compared across baselines and models — this is a standard privacy-utility trade-off evaluation design. The evaluation design (attack success rate + downstream utility across multiple models/datasets) is covered by [9] and [10].

Papers [10], [16], [20] all work in privacy-preserving NLP / text embedding privacy. Paper [16] explicitly studies information leakage in embedding models (NLP). Paper [10] addresses NLP privacy protection. This domain is clearly covered.
